summary: Herod Agrippa I attacks the Jerusalem community, executes James son of Zebedee, and imprisons Peter during the unleavened-bread festival. While the assembly prays, an angel leads Peter past guards and an iron gate. At Mary mother of John's house, the servant Rhoda recognizes Peter's voice but leaves him outside in her joy while the praying group disbelieves her. Peter directs that James and the believers be told, then departs. Herod executes the guards, travels to Caesarea, accepts divine honors during a political audience, and dies. Against royal violence and self-deification, the word of God grows and multiplies.
whyItMatters: Acts refuses a simplistic formula in which faithful prayer always produces the same temporal outcome: James is killed, Peter is delivered, guards die, and the community is both prayerful and incredulous. The chapter contrasts the fragile grandeur of a ruler who receives worship with the resilient growth of God's word, yet it does not make the collateral deaths easy.

context.author: The Luke–Acts narrator closing the Jerusalem-centered section under Herod Agrippa I
context.audience: Readers facing political violence, unanswered questions, surprising deliverance, and imperial pretension
context.date: Around AD 44, the year ancient sources place Agrippa I's death
context.setting: Jerusalem during Passover and Caesarea during a royal dispute with Tyre and Sidon
context.literaryForm: Persecution and prison-deliverance narrative followed by royal death and word-growth summary

outline.heading: Herod kills James and imprisons Peter while the church prays
An angel frees Peter and Rhoda announces him to the incredulous gathering
Herod accepts divine acclaim, dies, and the word multiplies

keyVerses.text: Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him.
keyVerses.why: The community's response to state violence is persistent intercession, though the chapter offers no mechanical guarantee.

keyVerses.text: When Peter had come to himself, he said, “Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.”
keyVerses.why: Peter recognizes deliverance only after moving through the bewildering escape.

keyVerses.text: But the word of God grew and multiplied.
keyVerses.why: The narrator contrasts the death of a self-exalting ruler with the continuing vitality of the word.

questions.question: Which Herod is this?
questions.answer: This is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great and ruler of Judea under Rome from AD 41 to 44. He cultivated Jewish support and possessed royal authority under imperial patronage. Distinguishing the Herods matters: this is not the ruler at Jesus's birth or the tetrarch in Jesus's Galilean ministry.

questions.question: Why is James's death told in one sentence while Peter receives a long rescue story?
questions.answer: Luke gives no explanation for the asymmetry. James, one of the Twelve and brother of John, is executed; Peter is later freed while the community prays. The contrast blocks the claim that enough faith guarantees escape and prevents deliverance stories from becoming judgments against those who die. Acts remembers both martyrdom and rescue inside the same faithful community.

questions.question: What does the four-squad guard detail contribute?
questions.answer: Four groups of four soldiers likely rotated watches, while Peter is chained between two guards and others secure the door. The precision magnifies royal custody and makes human plotting an inadequate explanation for escape. It also makes Herod's later execution of the guards a horrifying exercise of Roman-era custodial liability.

questions.question: Why does Peter think the escape is a vision?
questions.answer: The angel's commands are concrete—rise, dress, put on sandals, wrap the cloak—yet Peter initially does not know the event is real. Only outside, after the angel departs, does he ‘come to himself.’ Luke allows bewilderment within divine deliverance; spiritual experience is not portrayed as instant total comprehension.

questions.question: Why is Rhoda's comic scene important?
questions.answer: Paidiskē can mean servant girl or young female slave. Rhoda correctly recognizes Peter's voice and joyfully announces him, while the praying community calls her mad and proposes it is ‘his angel.’ Luke places reliable perception in a socially low-status woman and gently exposes believers who pray for rescue but cannot recognize the answer at their door.

questions.question: Who is the James Peter asks them to tell?
questions.answer: James son of Zebedee has just been killed, so this is James the brother of Jesus, emerging as a leading figure in Jerusalem. The concise instruction anticipates his role in Acts 15 and 21. Peter's departure and James's prominence show leadership becoming less centered on one apostle.

questions.question: Why are the guards executed for an angelic escape?
questions.answer: Ancient custodians could bear the penalty assigned to escaped prisoners, and Herod orders the guards killed after examination. The narrative reports this legal brutality without saying God desired their deaths. Rescue for Peter creates a morally troubling consequence under Herod's regime; honest reading should name the victims rather than treat them as scenery.

questions.question: How does Herod's death compare with Josephus?
questions.answer: Josephus also places Agrippa's fatal illness at Caesarea during a public festival, after royal splendor prompts divine acclamation; he describes sudden abdominal pain and death five days later. Acts interprets the event as angelic judgment because Herod accepts glory belonging to God. The accounts share a striking public core while differing in theological detail and timing.

questions.question: Why does Acts say the word ‘grew and multiplied’?
questions.answer: Growth and multiplication normally describe living populations. Luke personifies the logos of God so the message appears as the real expanding actor while Herod dies. This summary also links back to earlier Jerusalem growth and forward to Barnabas and Saul's mission.

glossary.def: Client king and grandson of Herod the Great who ruled Judea under Rome and died in AD 44.
